planting.note: Set out in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil with light shade while young so roots establish before the first cold snap.

directions: Native to high-elevation monsoon forest on Doi Chiang Dao and other Thai mountains, this species tolerates cold surprisingly well for a tropical-latitude palm, shrugging off brief drops into the low-to-mid teens Fahrenheit once established. It differs from Trachycarpus fortunei in its smaller stature, finer and more numerous leaf segments, and a slower, more compact growth habit that makes it a good choice where space is limited. Give it partial shade and consistent moisture as a juvenile, since it comes from a wetter monsoon climate than the drier Chinese habitats of its more common relatives, then shift toward full sun as it matures and trunks. Its seasonally wet-summer, dry-winter native climate also makes it noticeably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than some other high-elevation windmill palms.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

planting.note: Plant in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil once nights stay reliably above the mid-30s Fahrenheit; this species is less cold-tolerant than most other Braheas in cultivation.

directions: Named for the sharp, tooth-like spines lining its petiole margins, this tropical deciduous-forest native of Sinaloa, Mexico grows a taller, more solitary trunk than its shrubbier Brahea cousins and carries deep green to olive fronds rather than the powdery silver-blue typical of Brahea armata. It is markedly less cold-hardy than Brahea armata, decumbens, or moorei, generally suffering damage below the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit, so it suits the milder end of the Gulf Coast palm range rather than colder inland zone 8 sites. Once established it is quite drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil, but resents heavy or waterlogged ground. Handle young plants carefully when transplanting given the sharp petiole spines that give the species its name.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

planting.note: Install in full sun with plenty of overhead room in the warm months; this Caribbean species wants a milder, more protected site than mainland Sabal species.

directions: Endemic to the limestone hills of Hispaniola, this tall, solitary-trunked sabal is prized for the persistent diamond-patterned pattern of old leaf-base scars ('boots') that clothes its trunk for years before eventually sloughing off to reveal a smooth gray column beneath. Its finely divided, strongly costapalmate leaves and generally narrower crown distinguish it from the stockier, thicker-trunked Sabal causiarum and the shorter, coastal Sabal palmetto already common on the Gulf Coast. It is noticeably more cold-sensitive than native Gulf Coast sabals, so reserve it for zone 9b-11 sites or give it hard-freeze protection further north. Give it ample lateral and overhead space, since young plants are slow to trunk but eventually form one of the most striking specimen sabals available.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; established plants handle both drought and occasional hard freezes better than many other Mexican Pacific-slope palms.

directions: Native to seasonally dry tropical deciduous forest along Mexico's Pacific slope in Jalisco, Nayarit, and Colima, this sabal carries finely textured, strongly silvery-blue-green costapalmate leaves on a moderate, fiber-covered trunk. It is more drought-adapted than the Gulf Coast native Sabal palmetto and Sabal minor, reflecting its dry-forest origin, yet it has proven root-hardy into the low 20s Fahrenheit in cultivation trials, making it a reasonable candidate for zone 8 gardens willing to accept some top damage in hard winters. Its blue-green color and finer leaf segmentation give it a more refined, silvery look than the plain green of Sabal mexicana. Use it in xeriscape or dry-garden palm plantings where its drought tolerance and cold resilience both come into play.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms
